Earth & Luna wells amplified ×20,000 · heights, sizes and lunar separation illustrative.

From a curved grid to curved spacetime

In general relativity, matter and energy shape spacetime, and freely falling test bodies follow its geodesics. This picture is a visual analogy: the grid uses localized, potential-shaped depressions to illustrate deformation. It is not a literal shape of spacetime, a time axis, or an exact general-relativistic solution.

The Sun is roughly 333,000 times as massive as Earth. Choose Real mass ratio to see why Earth’s well is hard to distinguish on this scale. The amplified views apply the same gain to Earth and Luna’s contributions. All views retain enlarged body sizes and smoothed well centers. Grid depth changes the drawing only.

Earth’s blue orbit and center follow the Sun-only surface. Luna’s silver orbit and center follow the combined Sun-and-Earth surface. Each body’s own well extends beneath it. The Sun stays at the reference height above its depression. This is a drawing convention: bodies are not physically rolling on a sheet, and gravity has no well edge. Our smooth display boundaries are not physical cutoffs.

The circular guides have periods of 365.256 days for Earth and 27.3217 days for Luna, with one Earth year lasting 24 seconds at 1× speed. Luna’s orbit is enlarged for visibility; its actual mean distance from Earth is 384,400 km. Sizes and heights are illustrative. The orbits are prescribed, not calculated from the drawn wells. Orbital eccentricity, inclination, and Earth–Moon barycentric motion are omitted. Year position selects a time in the first model year; playback continues smoothly into subsequent years.
